newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr coasts on US$, races before yen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr coasts on US$, races before yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar put in another steady performance on its U.S. counterpart Wednesday as a generally upbeat market waited for recent gains to be fully absorbed before testing major resistance at US$0.8150.

Traders said bulls were again frustrated by options-related sales close to US$0.8130, but had so far found good support around US$0.8075 which convinced most dealers that any further dip should be regarded as a buying opportunity.
Sentiment was bolstered by a subdued Japanese Tankan survey of business sentiment which suggested interest rates there would be staying at record lows well into next year.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was coasting at US$0.8095/00 after steering in a narrow US$0.8086/8115 range all day and against a US$0.8100/05 close here Tuesday.
On the crosses it bounded to 91.56/66 yen, its best finish since September 1992, from 91.10/20 late Tuesday.
The latest rise brought the dollar's gains this year to a massive 15 yen, or 19 percent, an ascent largely fuelled by Japanese retail investors seeking a higher yielding home abroad.
One of the most popular vehicles for the journey were dual currency samurai bonds -- a record 308.5 billion yen had been launched so far in November and a sizeable chunk were yen/A$.
These tended to have high credit ratings, unlike some straight samurai issues, and offered returns of 5.25 percent or more against comparable Japanese yields of under one percent.
One potential threat to all this was a tightening in Japanese monetary policy which would herald a major shift in world capital flows, probably to the detriment of high yielders.

Which was why dollar bulls were relieved when the Bank of Japan's business sentiment survey showed conditions improved only modestly in Q3 with the diffusion index at minus three from minus seven. They noted the BOJ has never raised rates while the main index was in negative territory.
Instead, Japanese rates looked set to remain at record lows for some time yet with industry expecting the main index to stay in negative territory for the next quarter as well.
"There is no risk of a BOJ tightening on these figures," said Richard Gibbs, international economist at Macquarie Bank.
"The recovery in the economy is only very gradual and the sombre tone surrounding the financial sector all suggest there is no urgency on the policy front," he said.
That meant the A$'s yield advantage looked safe for a few months yet, which was timely as Japanese workers received winter bonuses over the next few weeks.
Analysts noted the man on the street had been the big investor in samurais up to now as life offices had steered clear due to the memory of huge currency losses in the early 1990's.

That might be about to chnage, however. Meiji Life, for instance, today said it panned to spend 300 billion yen on foreign bonds in the second half of 1996/97 compared with just 70 billion on domestic issues.
"If the life guys ever started to shift even a fraction fo their funds toward A$ assets the market, and the currency, would explode," said one hopeful dealer.
There were no data today but the Department of Industrial Relations should release its September quarter report on wage trends in enterprise bargains on Thursday morning.
These figures were largely ignored in the past but have risen to prominence because the Reserve Bank made a point of warning that some of the deals were running above its comfort zone in Q2.
Then the average annualised wage increase was 5.6 percent up from 4.7 in Q1, while growth for the private sector alone was a potentially inflationary 6.6 percent.
However, settlements were boosted by high agreements in the banking sector and excluding these wages had been rising by a more reasonable 4.5 and 5.2 percent, respectively.

Analysts expected some slowing in Q3, if only because one inflated bank agreement would be included as opposed to three in Q2, and a dip in the overall rate to below 5.0 percent would probably be taken by the bond market as good reason to expect another cut in interest rates.
